subject: environmental-systems

questions.content: What does the term biodiversity mean?
options: The number of individuals of one species
The variety of living things in an area, including species and genetic variety
The total mass of living things in an ecosystem
The size of a nature reserve
questions.explanation: Biodiversity is the variety of life, often described at the level of genes, species and ecosystems.

questions.content: What is species richness?
options: How many individuals of each species are present
How evenly individuals are spread between species
The number of different species in an area
The total area of a habitat
questions.explanation: Species richness is the count of different species. It does not describe how many individuals each species has.

questions.content: Which sampling tool is most suitable for estimating the number of daisies on a school field?
options: Quadrat
Pitfall trap
Kick net
Light meter
questions.explanation: A quadrat is a square frame used to sample plants and other organisms that do not move.

questions.content: Why are quadrats placed at random positions in a habitat?
options: To make the survey quicker
To count only the common species
To make sure at least one quadrat is in shade
To avoid bias, so the sample represents the whole area
questions.explanation: Random placement means the researcher's choices do not influence which areas are sampled, so results are more representative.

questions.content: Site A has 12 species and Site B has 5 species. Which statement is correct?
options: Site B has greater species richness
Site A has greater species richness
Both sites have the same species richness
Site B is more even
questions.explanation: Richness is the number of species, so Site A (12) has higher richness than Site B (5).

questions.content: A student counts clover plants in five 1 m² quadrats: 3, 5, 2, 4 and 6. The field is 200 m². What is the best estimate of the clover population?

In a capture-mark-recapture study, 40 beetles are marked and released. A later sample catches 30 beetles, of which 6 are marked. Using population = (marked × second sample) ÷ marked recaptured, what is the estimate?
questions.explanation: 40 × 30 ÷ 6 = 200 beetles. The recaptured fraction (6 of 30) suggests the marked beetles are one fifth of the population.

questions.content: Site A has 20 individuals in 4 species, with counts of 10, 6, 3 and 1. Site B has 20 individuals in 4 species, with counts of 17, 1, 1 and 1. Which conclusion is best?
options: Site B is more diverse because it has one large population
Both sites have the same diversity
Site B has more species
Site A is more diverse because individuals are more evenly spread among species
questions.explanation: Both sites have four species, so richness is equal. Site A has a more even spread (50%, 30%, 15% and 5% of individuals), while Site B is dominated by one species (85%).

questions.content: Two woodlands each contain four tree species. Woodland X has 25 trees of each species. Woodland Y has 97 trees of one species and 1 tree of each of the others. What is the difference between them?
options: Y has greater species richness
They have the same richness but X has greater evenness
X has fewer species
They are identical in diversity
questions.explanation: Richness is the same (four species), but X is even and Y is dominated by one species. Diversity indices consider both richness and evenness.

questions.content: A researcher wants to see how species change from the sea edge up a sand dune. Which method is best?
options: A line transect with quadrats at regular intervals
A single quadrat at the top
A kick sample
A pitfall trap in the car park
questions.explanation: A transect samples along a line across an environmental gradient, so changes in species can be linked to changes in conditions.

questions.content: Mayfly larvae are found in a stream. Why might an ecologist use them as an indicator species?
options: They are the largest animals in the stream
They are easy to catch with a net
They are sensitive to pollution, so their presence suggests clean, oxygen-rich water
They are present in all water, polluted or clean
questions.explanation: Indicator species have tolerance limits. Mayfly larvae need well-oxygenated water, so their presence shows good quality.

questions.content: When sampling stream invertebrates by kick sampling, why is each site sampled for exactly three minutes?
options: Longer would damage the net
Three minutes catches every animal
Animals only live for three minutes
A standard effort makes results from different sites comparable
questions.explanation: Keeping time, net size and method the same means differences in results are more likely to be real differences between sites.

questions.content: In a survey, 95% of all the individuals counted belong to a single species. What does this suggest about the community?
options: The site has very high diversity
The community is dominated by one or very few species
No species are present
Species are perfectly even
questions.explanation: When almost all individuals belong to one species, the community is uneven and dominated by that species. Its diversity is low, even if a few rare species are also present.

questions.content: A sample contains 16 individuals: 8 of species P, 4 of Q, 2 of R and 2 of S. What percentage of the sample is species P, and what does this show?
options: 50%, so P is dominant and the community is uneven even though four species are present
25%, so the four species are perfectly even
8%, so P is a rare species
200%, so P is the only species present
questions.explanation: 8 ÷ 16 × 100 = 50%. Half of all individuals belong to one species, so the community is uneven, although species richness is still four.

questions.content: In a capture-mark-recapture study, which assumption must be true for the estimate to be reliable?
options: Marking makes animals easier for predators to see
Marked animals stay in one corner of the habitat
Marking does not harm the animals, and marked individuals mix evenly with the population with no migration in or out
Only female animals should be marked
questions.explanation: If marking changes survival, or marked animals do not mix or the population changes through migration, the recaptured fraction will not represent the population.

questions.content: A survey of one 100 m² plot finds 14 plant species in a native woodland and 5 in a nearby pine plantation. A student concludes that all native woodlands are more diverse than all plantations. Which is the best evaluation?
options: The conclusion is valid because 14 is bigger than 5
The conclusion is invalid because richness cannot be measured
The conclusion is valid because woodlands are older
The conclusion is not supported: only one pair of sites was sampled once, so it cannot be generalised
questions.explanation: A general claim needs repeated sampling of many sites. One plot at each site shows a difference at those places only.

questions.content: Quadrat counts of a plant vary widely between quadrats (0, 12, 1, 9, 0, 14). What is the best way to improve the reliability of the density estimate?
options: Use more randomly placed quadrats
Use only the highest counts
Remove the zero counts
Use one larger quadrat in the densest patch
questions.explanation: A larger sample reduces the effect of chance and gives a more reliable mean. Removing data points or choosing dense areas introduces bias.

questions.content: A student places 25 quadrats (1 m² each) along the edge of a path in a 400 m² field and counts 75 daisies. She multiplies the mean by the area. What is the best evaluation of her estimate?
options: 3 daisies, because the mean is the population
1200 daisies, but likely an overestimate because the quadrats were not placed at random across the field
1200 daisies, which is certainly accurate
75 daisies, because that is the total counted
questions.explanation: Mean = 75 ÷ 25 = 3 per m². 3 × 400 = 1200. However, quadrats placed along the path may not represent the whole field, so the estimate is probably biased.

note:
## What is biodiversity?
**Biodiversity** is the variety of life. It can be described at three levels: **genetic diversity** (variation within a species), **species diversity** (the variety of species in an area) and **ecosystem diversity** (the variety of habitats). Scientists measure biodiversity so they can compare places, track change over time and decide which areas most need protection.

## Richness and evenness
- **Species richness** is the number of different species in an area.
- **Species evenness** is how similar the numbers of individuals of each species are.

Two sites can have the same richness but very different diversity. A meadow with 100 individuals spread equally over four species is more diverse than one with 97 of one species and one of each of the other three. Diversity measures use both ideas.

## Sampling methods
Because we cannot count every organism, we take samples.
- **Quadrats**: a square frame placed on the ground to count plants or slow-moving animals. Use random positions (for example, random coordinates) to avoid bias.
- **Transects**: a line across a habitat with samples at regular intervals. Good for showing changes along a gradient such as the shore, a hillside or a path.
- **Kick sampling**: a net held downstream while you kick the stream bed for a set time (for example three minutes) to collect invertebrates.
- **Pitfall traps** and **pooters** collect ground insects.
- **Capture-mark-recapture** is used for mobile animals. Population = (number marked first × size of second sample) ÷ number of marked animals recaptured. Example: 40 marked, second sample 30 with 6 marked: 40 × 30 ÷ 6 = 200. Assumptions: marking does not harm the animals, marked animals mix back in evenly and there is no migration, birth or death between samples.

## Estimating a population from quadrats
Mean density = total number counted ÷ number of quadrats. Population estimate = mean density × total area ÷ quadrat area. Example: counts of 3, 5, 2, 4, 6 in 1 m² quadrats give a mean of 4 per m². In a 200 m² field the estimate is 800.

## Comparing diversity using relative abundance
To compare how even two communities are, work out the percentage of all individuals that each species makes up: species count ÷ total individuals × 100. Example: counts of 10, 6, 3 and 1 (total 20) give 50%, 30%, 15% and 5%. Counts of 17, 1, 1 and 1 (total 20) give 85%, 5%, 5% and 5%. Both sites have four species, but the second is dominated by one species, so it is less even and less diverse. If one species makes up almost all of a sample, diversity is low.

## Indicator species
Some species are sensitive to pollution, so their presence or absence suggests environmental quality. Lichens indicate clean air, and mayfly larvae suggest clean, oxygen-rich water. Rat-tailed maggots and sludge worms can survive in polluted, low-oxygen water.

## Improving reliability
Use random sampling, enough samples, the same method and time at each site, and repeat. Keep variables such as quadrat size and season constant. Say what could cause error, such as animals escaping or misidentified species.

## Common mistakes
- Saying richness and diversity are the same thing. Diversity includes evenness.
- Placing quadrats where there are more plants and calling it random.
- Forgetting to multiply the mean by the total area, or dividing by the wrong quadrat size.

## How this is examined
You may get a table of species counts from two sites, a description of a survey method, and be asked to calculate a mean density, population estimate or the percentage of each species, compare sites, and evaluate the reliability and limitations of the sampling.

Exam tip: when asked to evaluate a survey, comment on sample size, randomness, repeats and whether the conclusion can be generalised beyond the sites sampled.

flashcards.back: The variety of life in an area, including genetic diversity, species diversity and ecosystem diversity.
Richness is the number of different species. Evenness is how equal the numbers of individuals are between species.
To avoid bias, so the sample represents the whole habitat and the results are more reliable.
Mean number per quadrat ÷ quadrat area × total area of the habitat.
Population = (number marked first × size of second sample) ÷ number of marked animals in the second sample.
Number of one species ÷ total number of individuals × 100. If one species makes up most of the sample, the community is uneven and less diverse.
A species whose presence or absence shows environmental quality, for example lichens (clean air) or mayfly larvae (clean water).
To sample along a line across a gradient, such as from the sea up a dune, so changes in species can be linked to changing conditions.
Marking is harmless, marked animals mix evenly with the population, and there is no migration, birth or death between samples.

subject: environmental-systems

questions.content: Which human activity is considered the leading cause of biodiversity loss worldwide?
options: Destruction and degradation of habitats
Increased tourism
Planting trees
Using renewable energy
questions.explanation: Clearing land for farming, buildings and roads removes the places where species live, and is the largest single cause of biodiversity loss.

questions.content: What is an invasive species?
options: Any species with a small population
A species that has recently evolved
A non-native species that spreads and harms the native community
A species that is hunted by humans
questions.explanation: Invasive species are introduced to a new area, spread quickly and damage native species or ecosystems.

questions.content: A species is described as extinct. What does this mean?
options: Its numbers are falling
It only lives in zoos
It lives in only one country
No individuals of the species remain alive anywhere
questions.explanation: Extinction means the whole species has died out. Species that survive only in captivity are called extinct in the wild.

questions.content: Which of these is an example of overexploitation?
options: Planting a hedgerow
Catching fish faster than their populations can replace themselves
Building a nature reserve
Reintroducing wolves
questions.explanation: Overexploitation means harvesting a resource, such as fish, timber or wildlife, faster than it can be replaced.

questions.content: How does climate change threaten coral reefs?
options: It makes oceans too cold
It increases the amount of salt in sand
Warmer water can cause corals to expel their algae and bleach
It stops fish from breathing air
questions.explanation: When the water is too warm, corals expel the symbiotic algae that give them colour and food. This is bleaching and it can kill the coral.

questions.content: A forest of 500 km² loses 12% of its area to farming. How much forest remains?
options: 60 km²
380 km²
488 km²
440 km²
questions.explanation: 12% of 500 = 60 km² lost. 500 − 60 = 440 km² remains.

questions.content: A square reserve measures 10 km by 10 km (area 100 km², perimeter 40 km). It is split by roads into four separate 5 km by 5 km squares. What happens to the total length of edge?
options: It stays the same at 40 km
It doubles to 80 km, giving more edge habitat and exposure to outside effects
It halves to 20 km
It falls to zero
questions.explanation: Each small square has a perimeter of 20 km, and 4 × 20 = 80 km. More edge means more exposure to wind, predators and invasive species, and less core habitat.

questions.content: Why are island species often especially vulnerable to an introduced predator such as a cat or rat?
options: Island species are always smaller
Predators cannot swim to islands
They often evolved without such predators and have few defences
Islands have no food for predators
questions.explanation: Many island species lost defences such as flight or fear of predators because there were none. Introduced predators can drive them to extinction quickly.

questions.content: An insecticide that does not break down washes into a pond. Later, fish-eating birds lay eggs with thin shells that break easily. What is the best explanation?
options: The birds are eating too much calcium
The pesticide accumulates in food chains and affects the birds' reproduction
The pond has too much oxygen
The birds have been hunted too much
questions.explanation: Persistent chemicals build up in tissues and get more concentrated at higher trophic levels. Some caused eggshell thinning in birds of prey and fish-eating birds.

questions.content: A population of a rare frog falls from 2400 to 1800 over five years. What is the percentage decrease?
questions.explanation: The decrease is 600. 600 ÷ 2400 × 100 = 25%. Using 1800 as the base gives 33%, which is incorrect.

questions.content: Why is a specialist species, such as an animal that eats only one kind of bamboo, more at risk than a generalist?
options: Specialists are always larger
It depends on a single resource, so losing that resource could cause its extinction
Specialists reproduce too quickly
Generalists have smaller ranges
questions.explanation: A specialist has a narrow niche. If its food or habitat disappears it cannot easily switch to something else.

questions.content: High demand for rhino horn and elephant ivory has led to illegal hunting. Which threat does this represent?
options: Pollution
Habitat fragmentation
Invasive species
Overexploitation
questions.explanation: Poaching harvests wild animals faster than populations can recover. This is overexploitation, driven by market demand.

questions.content: Why does a very small population of a rare animal face extra danger even if its habitat is protected?
options: Small populations eat more food
Small populations have low genetic variety, so inbreeding and disease can have a large effect
Small populations are always invasive
Small populations cause habitat loss
questions.explanation: With few individuals, mates are related, harmful traits become common and a disease or bad year can wipe out the population.

questions.content: Researchers list the threats to 200 endangered species: habitat loss affects 120, overexploitation 70, invasive species 50 and pollution 40. The total is 280. A student says there is an error. What is the best response?
options: Yes, because the total must not exceed 200
Yes, because pollution cannot affect species
No, because habitat loss is the only real threat
No, because many species face more than one threat, so counts overlap
questions.explanation: Most species face several threats at once, so the counts add up to more than the number of species. Percentages of species affected would not total 100%.

questions.content: A student claims: "Introduced species always damage ecosystems." Which is the most accurate evaluation?
options: The claim is correct because every introduced species is invasive
The claim is incorrect because introduced species never spread
The claim is overgeneralised: many introduced species fail to establish or have little effect, and only some become invasive
The claim is correct because native species never compete
questions.explanation: Only a fraction of introduced species establish and spread enough to cause harm. Cane toads in Australia are an example of one that did.

questions.content: A forest of 1200 ha loses 60 ha each year. If this constant loss continues, after how many years will 300 ha remain?
options: 5 years
20 years
10 years
15 years
questions.explanation: The area to be lost is 1200 − 300 = 900 ha. 900 ÷ 60 = 15 years. The whole forest would be gone in 20 years.

questions.content: A road splits a reserve in two. Ten years later, the mouse populations on each side are small and genetically different from each other. Which explanation is best?
options: Mice have stopped breeding
The road has increased the food supply
The mice have evolved wings
The road is a barrier that reduces movement and gene flow between the two populations
questions.explanation: Fragmentation isolates populations. With little movement between them, genetic variety within each falls and the groups drift apart.

questions.content: Rainforest is cleared for oil palm plantations. Which statement best explains why this causes a major loss of biodiversity?
options: Palms release too much oxygen
Rainforest has few species, so little is lost
A plantation of one crop species offers far fewer niches, food sources and shelter than a forest with many species
Plantations always increase rainfall
questions.explanation: A monoculture supports far fewer species than diverse forest. It also removes habitat for species that need the original forest structure.

note:
## Why is biodiversity declining?
Species have always gone extinct naturally, but today the rate of loss is far higher than the natural background rate. Almost all of this increase is linked to human activity. A useful way to remember the main threats is the **HIPPO** list: **H**abitat loss, **I**nvasive species, **P**ollution, **P**opulation growth (human) and **O**verexploitation. Climate change is now often added as a major threat.

## Habitat loss and fragmentation
Clearing forests, draining wetlands and building cities removes habitats completely. Where some habitat remains it is often broken into small pieces. This is **fragmentation**. Fragments have:
- more **edge** and less core habitat, so organisms are more exposed to wind, heat, predators and invasive species;
- smaller populations that are isolated, so there is less movement of individuals and genes;
- greater risk of local extinction because small populations are vulnerable to disease and bad years.

Example: a 10 km by 10 km square reserve has an edge of 40 km. Split it into four 5 km squares and the total edge is 80 km, although the area is unchanged.

## Invasive species
Species moved to new places, deliberately or by accident, can become invasive. They may eat or outcompete native species, spread disease, or change the habitat. Invasive species often have no natural predators or diseases in their new home. Island species are especially vulnerable because they evolved without predators such as rats and cats. Only some introduced species become invasive, so avoid saying that all do.

## Overexploitation
Harvesting wild species faster than they can reproduce causes populations to collapse. Examples include overfishing, illegal hunting for ivory and rhino horn, and the collecting of rare plants. The passenger pigeon, once among the most numerous birds in North America, was hunted to extinction by 1914.

## Pollution
Chemicals such as pesticides, plastics and fertiliser runoff harm organisms directly or accumulate in food chains. Persistent pesticides caused eggshell thinning in some birds of prey. Nutrient pollution can cause oxygen loss in water.

## Climate change
Rising temperatures and changing rainfall alter habitats faster than many species can adapt or move. Warm oceans cause coral bleaching, and melting sea ice removes habitat for polar species. Specialist species and those on mountain tops or islands have nowhere to go.

## Vulnerable species
Species are more at risk if they are specialists, have small populations, have a small range, reproduce slowly, or are large predators needing big territories. Small populations lose genetic diversity, which makes inbreeding and disease more damaging.

## Worked example
A frog population falls from 2400 to 1800. Percentage decrease = (2400 − 1800) ÷ 2400 × 100 = 25%. Always divide by the original value.

## Common mistakes
- Saying all introduced species are invasive.
- Treating threats as separate when they often combine.
- Calculating a percentage change from the new value rather than the original.

## How this is examined
Questions may give a case study, such as a forest cleared for farming or an island with introduced predators, plus data on area or population. You may need to identify the threats, calculate the change, explain how the threat reduces biodiversity, and evaluate which is the most serious.

Exam tip: link each threat to a mechanism. For example, say fragmentation reduces gene flow because populations are isolated, not just that it is bad.

flashcards.back: A memory aid for the main threats: Habitat loss, Invasive species, Pollution, Population growth (human) and Overexploitation.
Breaking up a large habitat into small isolated pieces, which increases edge effects and reduces gene flow between populations.
A non-native species that spreads and harms native species or ecosystems, often because it has no natural predators in its new home.
Harvesting a species faster than it can reproduce, for example overfishing or poaching for ivory.
They often evolved without predators or competitors, so introduced species such as rats and cats can quickly drive them to extinction.
A persistent chemical builds up in tissues and becomes more concentrated at each higher trophic level of a food chain.
Warm water causes corals to expel their symbiotic algae, so they turn white and may die.

flashcards.front: Why do small populations face extra risk?
flashcards.back: Low genetic variety causes inbreeding, and disease or a bad year can wipe them out.
(original − new) ÷ original × 100. Always divide by the original value.

subject: environmental-systems

questions.content: Which of these is an example of ex situ conservation?
options: A national park
A marine protected area
A wildlife corridor
A seed bank
questions.explanation: Ex situ means "off site": protecting species outside their natural habitat, for example in zoos, botanic gardens and seed banks.

questions.content: Which of these is an example of in situ conservation?
options: A zoo breeding programme
Establishing a protected national park
Freezing seeds in a vault
Storing animal cells in a lab
questions.explanation: In situ means "on site": protecting species in their natural habitat.

questions.content: What does the agreement known as CITES regulate?
options: Fishing quotas in the Atlantic
The use of fertilisers
International trade in endangered species and their products
Emissions from cars
questions.explanation: CITES controls the international trade of wild animals and plants to make sure trade does not threaten their survival.

questions.content: What is the main purpose of a wildlife corridor?
options: Connect separated habitats so animals can move between them
Provide a place for tourists to camp
Keep predators out of a reserve
Increase the amount of fertiliser in soil
questions.explanation: Corridors link fragments of habitat, helping animals find food and mates and allowing gene flow between populations.

questions.content: Which IUCN Red List category describes a species facing a very high risk of extinction in the wild, but not yet critically?
options: Least Concern
Endangered
Vulnerable
Extinct
questions.explanation: The order of threat runs: Least Concern, Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered, Extinct in the Wild, Extinct. Endangered is higher risk than Vulnerable.

questions.content: A zoo breeds endangered parrots for release. Which is a limitation of captive breeding?
options: Parrots can never reproduce in zoos
It always damages wild habitats
Captive-bred animals may lack skills for the wild and the breeding group may have little genetic variety
It is always cheaper than protecting habitat
questions.explanation: Animals bred in captivity may not know how to find food or avoid predators, and a small founder group limits genetic diversity.

questions.content: A fishing authority sets a quota on the total weight of cod that can be caught each year. How does this support conservation?
options: It lets fishers take unlimited cod
It limits harvesting so the fish population can reproduce and recover
It bans all fishing forever
It increases the numbers of predators
questions.explanation: A quota is a limit set so that catches stay at or below the level the population can replace, supporting sustainable use.

questions.content: A village is given the right to manage a forest and share income from sustainable tourism. Why can this community-based approach help conservation?
options: It removes all rules
It stops all income
Local people gain a direct benefit from protecting the forest, so they are more likely to support it
It forces people to leave the area
questions.explanation: When local people benefit economically they have a reason to protect wildlife. Conservation that ignores local needs often fails.

questions.content: Programme A spends $240 000 to protect 600 ha. Programme B spends $450 000 to protect 1500 ha. Which has the lower cost per hectare?
options: Programme A, at $400 per hectare
They are equal
Neither, because cost per hectare cannot be calculated
Programme B, at $300 per hectare
questions.explanation: A: 240 000 ÷ 600 = $400 per ha. B: 450 000 ÷ 1500 = $300 per ha. B is cheaper per hectare, although cost is only one factor.

questions.content: Ecotourism is promoted as a conservation tool. Which statement shows a possible problem with it?
options: It creates no jobs
It can bring disturbance, waste and development if visitor numbers are not controlled
It lowers awareness of wildlife
It always protects every species
questions.explanation: Ecotourism can fund protection, but large numbers of visitors may disturb animals, create pollution and damage habitats.

questions.content: Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in the mid-1990s. Which result is an example of how the strategy can restore ecosystem balance?
options: Deer and elk numbers and behaviour changed, allowing vegetation to recover in some areas
Wolves removed all other predators
Plants stopped growing
Rivers dried up
questions.explanation: Predator reintroduction can reduce overgrazing, giving plants a chance to regrow. It is a rewilding approach, and results are complex and debated.

questions.content: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway stores duplicates of seeds from gene banks around the world. What is its main aim?
options: To grow food for Norway
To sell seeds to farmers
To protect crop genetic diversity as a back-up against loss
To plant forests in the Arctic
questions.explanation: Seed banks preserve genetic variety for future breeding and as insurance against disasters, war or disease.

questions.content: What is a no-take zone within a marine protected area?
options: An area where tourists are not allowed to swim
An area where fishing and extraction of marine life are banned, allowing populations to recover
An area where only large boats may fish
An area where waste is dumped
questions.explanation: In a no-take zone nothing can be removed. Fish can grow larger and breed, and some may move out to nearby fishing areas.

questions.content: A captive breeding programme releases 30 animals into the wild after beginning with 12 breeding animals. What is the percentage increase from 12 to 30?
questions.explanation: The increase is 30 − 12 = 18. 18 ÷ 12 × 100 = 150%. A 250% value is the 30 compared as a percentage of 12, not the increase.

questions.content: A habitat is nearly destroyed and only 40 individuals of a species remain. Which strategy combination is best justified?
options: Do nothing, as natural selection will solve the problem
Only ex situ conservation for ever
Only create more roads through the habitat
Protect and restore remaining habitat (in situ) and run a captive breeding programme as a back-up (ex situ), with careful planning for reintroduction
questions.explanation: Ex situ methods provide security while in situ work restores habitat. Without habitat the animals have nowhere to be released.

questions.content: A fish stock of 50 000 grows by 12% each year if left alone. Fishers take 8000 in one year. What is the stock at the end of the year, assuming growth is added before the catch?
questions.explanation: Growth = 12% of 50 000 = 6000, so the stock becomes 56 000. After taking 8000 it is 48 000. The catch is higher than the growth, so the stock is falling and the harvest is not sustainable.

questions.content: A government announces a "protected area" but there are few rangers and logging continues. A student says the area is not effective. Which evidence would best support the student's claim?
options: The area has a sign at the entrance
The area is large
Satellite images show forest cover continuing to fall inside the boundary
The area is mentioned in a speech
questions.explanation: Effectiveness is judged by outcomes. If forest is still being lost, the protection exists on paper only, so it needs enforcement and resources.

questions.content: Should conservation funding go to one very large reserve or several small ones of the same total area? Which argument favours the single large reserve?
options: Small reserves have more core habitat
Large areas have less edge relative to area and can support bigger populations of species that need space
Small reserves cannot be fenced
Large reserves never need management
questions.explanation: A large reserve has proportionally less edge and supports larger, more genetically healthy populations. Several small reserves can spread risk, so the choice involves trade-offs.

note:
## Why conserve?
Conservation means protecting and managing species and ecosystems. People give several reasons: ecosystems provide services such as clean water, pollination and flood control; species have value for food, medicine and tourism; and many people feel that nature has its own right to exist. In MYP Sciences you should be able to describe strategies, evaluate their strengths and limits, and judge which is most suitable in a given case.

## In situ strategies (on site)
Protecting species in their natural habitat.
- **Protected areas** such as national parks, nature reserves and marine protected areas restrict harmful activities. They only work if rules are enforced and local people are involved.
- **Wildlife corridors** connect fragments so animals can move and genes can flow.
- **Habitat restoration and rewilding**: replanting forests, restoring wetlands, or reintroducing missing species. Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in the mid-1990s, and the effect on deer behaviour and vegetation has been studied.
- **Sustainable management**: fishing quotas, closed seasons and sustainable forestry let harvesting continue without collapsing populations.

## Ex situ strategies (off site)
Protecting species outside their natural habitat.
- **Captive breeding** in zoos and aquaria, with the aim to release animals later.
- **Seed banks and botanic gardens**, such as the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway, which stores back-up seed from around the world.
- **Gene banks** that freeze cells or sperm.

Limitations: captive animals may lose wild skills, the founder group may have little genetic variety, it is expensive, and there is no point releasing animals if their habitat has gone. Ex situ is best used as a back-up and alongside in situ work.

## Laws and agreements
International agreements such as **CITES** regulate trade in endangered species. National laws can ban hunting or protect habitats. Laws need monitoring, penalties and enough funding.

## Community involvement
People who live next to wildlife are more likely to protect it if they benefit, for example from ecotourism jobs or from managing resources sustainably. Ignoring local needs can lead to poaching and conflict. Ecotourism can fund conservation, but too many visitors can cause disturbance and waste.

## The IUCN Red List
This assesses extinction risk. Categories from lowest to highest risk: Least Concern, Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered, Extinct in the Wild, Extinct. It helps to decide which species need action first.

## Worked example: comparing costs
Programme A: $240 000 for 600 ha = $400 per ha. Programme B: $450 000 for 1500 ha = $300 per ha. B is cheaper per hectare, but you should also consider the quality of the habitat, the species protected and long-term running costs.

Sustainable harvest example: a fish stock of 50 000 grows 12% a year (6000). Taking 8000 means the stock falls to 48 000, so the catch is not sustainable. A sustainable catch is no more than the annual growth.

## Common mistakes
- Confusing in situ (on site) with ex situ (off site).
- Saying captive breeding alone saves a species. Habitat protection is also needed.
- Ignoring people. The best strategies consider local communities and economics.

## How this is examined
Questions usually give a species or region and ask you to recommend and justify strategies. You may need to calculate cost per hectare or population change, compare two options using stated criteria, and discuss limitations such as cost, enforcement and genetic diversity.

Exam tip: in an evaluation question give at least one strength and one limitation of each strategy, then make a clear judgement using evidence from the context.
